mainTopic: Sending a thigh with the גיד הנשה to a גוי, and the prohibition of גניבת דעת (misleading people, even a גוי).
overview: This amud has three parts. It opens by finishing a question about sending a גוי a thigh that still has the גיד הנשה in it: a whole thigh is allowed, but a cut one is not. The גמרא asks how that can be. Where they don't announce non-kosher sales (מקום שאין מכריזין), even a cut thigh should be fine. Where they do announce (מקום שמכריזין), even a whole thigh should be risky. It answers that in the second kind of place, meat cut by a גוי is easy to recognize. In the first kind of place, a cut thigh is banned by a גזירה, or because sending it would deceive the גוי, following שמואל's rule against גניבת דעת even toward a גוי. The גמרא then shows that שמואל's rule was only inferred from a story about a ferryman, and that each version of the story could be read another way. Next come ברייתות about other ways of misleading people: fake invitations, sold barrels, a half-empty jug for a mourner, a sandal from a dead animal, and a wine barrel topped with oil. Two tragic stories show how much harm such things can cause, and the גמרא shows that one whole ברייתא belongs to רבי אליעזר בן יעקב. Finally, a ברייתא returns to the גיד הנשה and to selling non-kosher meat to a גוי. The amud ends just as it begins a rule with two reasons, which are given on the next amud.

steps.title: If Jews never buy from the gentile, a cut thigh should be allowed too
steps.stepSummary: First side of the dilemma: in a place where Jews do not buy meat from a גוי, there is no risk, so even a cut thigh should be permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then even a cut thigh should be sent to him, because Jews do not come to buy from him anyway!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing the first half of a challenge. It argues that in a place where Jews never buy meat from a גוי, sending even a cut thigh should be fine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban on a cut thigh only makes sense if a Jew might later buy that meat from the גוי. In a place where Jews never buy meat from a גוי at all, that risk does not exist. So the distinction between a whole thigh and a cut one seems pointless there.

keyTerms.meaning: Cut up: a thigh that has been sliced, so the גיד הנשה is no longer easy to spot

steps.confusionAlert: This text starts in the middle of the question. The first half, about a place where they do not announce, comes just before it. So 'a cut thigh too' is talking about that kind of place.

phrases.english: Then even a cut one should be sent to him,
since they (Jews) do not come to buy from him!

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲתוּכָה נָמֵי לִישַׁדַּר לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the first side of a 'how do we picture this case' question that began before this text.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a whole thigh may be sent but a cut thigh may not.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Where Jews never buy meat from a גוי, there is no risk at all, so the ban on a cut thigh has no reason.

steps.title: If Jews do buy from the gentile, even a whole thigh should be forbidden
steps.stepSummary: Second side of the dilemma: in a place where Jews buy from a גוי, even a whole thigh is risky, because he could cut it up and sell it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if this is a place where they announce, then even a whole thigh should not be sent to him, because he will cut it and sell it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now tries the other kind of place, a מקום שמכריזין, where Jews do buy meat from a גוי. Here it argues that even a whole thigh should be forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a מקום שמכריזין, the Jewish butchers announce whenever they sell non-kosher meat to a גוי. So when there is no announcement, Jews feel free to buy meat from a גוי. The גוי could then cut up the whole thigh and sell it to a Jew who would not notice the גיד הנשה. So neither kind of place seems to fit the rule 'whole yes, cut no.'

keyTerms.meaning: In a place where they announce: the butchers announce whenever they sell non-kosher meat to a גוי, so otherwise Jews may buy meat from him

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a true dilemma. Each kind of place seems to break one half of the rule, so the גמרא has to explain how both halves can stand.

phrases.english: Rather, in a place where they announce,
phrases.notes: The announcement is made whenever non-kosher meat is sold to a גוי. With no announcement, Jews may buy his meat.

phrases.english: then even a whole one should not be sent to him,
since he will cut it and sell it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁמַּכְרִיזִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second side of the dilemma after the first side failed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a whole thigh may be sent to a גוי.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Where Jews buy from a גוי, he could cut the whole thigh and sell it to them, so a whole thigh is also risky.

steps.title: The answer can work in either kind of place
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא announces two possible answers, one for each kind of place. Each will be explained next.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say it is a place where they announce; and if you want, say it is a place where they do not announce.
steps.whatsHappening: This line is a setup. The גמרא says the משנה can be explained in either kind of place, and the next two steps will explain each option.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא does not pick one kind of place. Instead, it claims that the rule 'whole yes, cut no' can be defended in both kinds of place, each for its own reason.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say: a formula for offering two possible answers
In a place where they do not announce: Jews there do not buy meat from a גוי at all

phrases.english: If you wish, say: in a place where they announce;

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא – בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁאֵין מַכְרִיזִין.
phrases.english: and if you wish, say: in a place where they do not announce.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁמַּכְרִיזִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to both sides of the dilemma by offering two possible settings.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Two alternative answers, one for each kind of place.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Each kind of place seemed to contradict one half of the rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both kinds of place work, each for a different reason, explained in the next steps.

steps.title: Where they announce, a gentile's cutting is easy to recognize
steps.stepSummary: In a מקום שמכריזין, a whole thigh is allowed, because a Jew can tell that meat was cut by a גוי and will not buy it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say it is a place where they announce: the cutting of a גוי is easy to recognize.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the second side of the dilemma. Even where Jews buy from a גוי, a whole thigh is safe, because meat he cuts himself looks different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry was that the גוי would cut up the whole thigh and sell it. The answer is that Jewish butchers cut in a recognizable way. A piece cut by a גוי stands out, so a Jew will not buy it. A thigh that was already cut by a Jew before it was sent would not stand out this way, which is why a cut thigh stays forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: The cutting of a גוי: the way a non-Jew cuts meat

phrases.english: If you wish, say: in a place where they announce,
the cutting of a gentile is recognizable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁמַּכְרִיזִין חִיתּוּכָא דְּגוֹי מִידָּע יְדִיעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first of the two answers announced in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual answer: meat cut by a גוי can be recognized.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The גוי could cut a whole thigh and pass it off to a Jew.
steps.terutzMaskana: A Jew will recognize meat cut by a גוי, so sending a whole thigh is safe.

steps.title: Where they don't announce, a cut thigh is banned by decree
steps.stepSummary: In a מקום שאין מכריזין, a cut thigh is still forbidden by a גזירה, in case it is handed over in front of another Jew who would think it is kosher.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say it is a place where they do not announce: it is a decree, in case he gives it to the גוי in front of another Jew.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the first side of the dilemma. Even where Jews never buy from a גוי, a cut thigh is forbidden because of a rabbinic decree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The danger here is not the גוי reselling the meat. The danger is that another Jew might see a Jew hand over a cut, Jewish-cut piece of meat. He would assume it is kosher and might later buy it from the גוי. A whole thigh does not create this risk, because the גיד הנשה in it is easy to see.

keyTerms.meaning: A rabbinic decree made as a protective measure

steps.whatToRemember: A whole thigh may always be sent to a גוי, but a cut one may not. Where they announce, a whole thigh is safe because meat cut by a גוי is recognizable. Where they don't announce, a cut thigh is still banned by a גזירה, in case another Jew sees it handed over and thinks it is kosher.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say: in a place where they do not announce,
it is a decree, lest he give it to him
in the presence of another Jew.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁאֵין מַכְרִיזִין גְּזֵירָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the second of the two answers announced in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A rabbinic decree (גזירה) based on how things look to an onlooker.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Where Jews never buy from a גוי, a cut thigh should be allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: A cut thigh is still forbidden, because another Jew watching might think it is kosher and buy it.

steps.title: A second answer: sending a cut thigh deceives the גוי
steps.stepSummary: Instead of the גזירה from Step 5, the גמרא suggests a cut thigh is forbidden because sending it deceives the גוי. It backs this with שמואל's rule that one may not deceive anyone, even a גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you like, say the reason is that he is deceiving the גוי. As שמואל said: it is forbidden to deceive people, even a גוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a completely different reason why a cut thigh may not be sent to a גוי: it would be deceiving him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 worried about another Jew being misled. This answer looks at the גוי himself, who is being misled. The rule against deceiving people, called גניבת דעת, applies even to a גוי, so the cut thigh is forbidden for that reason alone.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say: introduces another possible answer
"Stealing someone's mind": deceiving a person or giving a false impression

steps.whyThisMatters: This step brings in a general ethical-halachic rule: you may not create a false impression, even toward a non-Jew and even without taking any money.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
because he is deceiving him,
phrases.notes: Literally "stealing his mind": giving him a false impression.

phrases.english: as שמואל said:
it is forbidden to deceive people,
and even a גוי.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא, מִשּׁוּם דְּקָא גָנֵיב לֵיהּ לְדַעְתֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different reason in place of the גזירה from Step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative reason (ethical prohibition rather than a protective גזירה)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The only problem with a cut thigh is that another Jew might be misled.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even without any risk to Jews, sending it deceives the גוי, and that is forbidden.

steps.title: שמואל's rule came from a story on a ferry
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that שמואל never stated this rule outright. It was worked out from a story: his attendant paid the ferryman, and שמואל got angry.
steps.simpleTranslation: This rule of שמואל was not said openly. It was worked out from an event. שמואל was crossing on a ferry and told his attendant, "Pay the ferryman." The attendant paid him, and שמואל got angry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells us where שמואל's rule really comes from: a story, not a direct statement. This sets up the next question about why שמואל got angry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A rule said openly is clear. A rule worked out from someone's behavior depends on guessing why he acted that way. Here we only know that שמואל got angry, not why. That opens the door to the questions that follow.

phrases.english: And this rule of שמואל
was not stated openly,
rather it was worked out by inference.
For שמואל was crossing on a ferry,
he said to his attendant:
"Pay the ferryman."
He paid him, and שמואל became angry.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא דִּשְׁמוּאֵל, לָאו בְּפֵירוּשׁ אִיתְּמַר, אֶלָּא מִכְּלָלָא אִיתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the source of the שמואל rule quoted in Step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שמואל's rule against deceiving people comes from a story about his anger at his attendant, not from a direct statement.

steps.title: Why did שמואל get angry?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the attendant did wrong that made שמואל angry.
steps.simpleTranslation: What was the reason he got angry?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a simple question about the story: what upset שמואל? This sets up the two answers that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule was worked out from this story, so everything depends on the reason for שמואל's anger. The story does not tell us, so the גמרא asks.

phrases.english: What was the reason he got angry?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא אִיקְּפַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the missing detail in the story from Step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the attendant did that upset שמואל.

steps.title: אביי: he passed off a טרפה chicken as kosher
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the attendant paid with a טרפה chicken and presented it as a properly slaughtered one.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: it was a טרפה chicken, and he gave it to the ferryman as if it were a kosher, slaughtered one.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question: the attendant gave the ferryman a non-kosher chicken while pretending it was kosher.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ferryman thought he was getting a better gift than he really was. That is deception, which fits שמואל's rule against fooling even a גוי.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect, forbidden to eat even if slaughtered

phrases.english: אביי said:
It was a טרפה chicken,
and he gave it to him as if it were a slaughtered, kosher one.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: תַּרְנְגוֹלֶת טְרֵפָה הֲוַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The attendant passed off a טרפה chicken as kosher.

steps.title: רבא: he served diluted wine in place of strong wine
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives a different version: שמואל told the attendant to give the ferryman wine from an אנפקא, but the attendant gave him watered-down wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: שמואל told him to give the ferryman a drink from an אנפקא, but he gave him diluted wine.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא offers a second explanation of what went wrong: the ferryman was given weaker wine than he was supposed to get.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רבא's version the problem is plainly deception, since the ferryman got watered-down wine when better was expected. Nothing forbidden is involved here, just giving a false impression.

keyTerms.meaning: A type of cup, used for undiluted, strong wine

phrases.english: רבא said:
He told him to give him a drink from an אנפקא,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording. Either way it means "to give him a drink."

phrases.english: but he gave him diluted wine to drink.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: אַנְפָּקָא אֲמַר לֵיהּ לְאַשְׁקוֹיֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to Step 8, alongside אביי's.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The attendant gave diluted wine when strong wine was intended.

steps.title: So what if the rule was only inferred?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why it matters that שמואל's rule came only by inference. Either way, the story seems to show the rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it was by inference, so what?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why it even pointed out that the rule was worked out from a story. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both אביי and רבא describe some kind of deception, so the rule seems proven either way. The גמרא wants to know what difference "only by inference" makes.

keyTerms.meaning: And if it was by inference, what of it?

phrases.english: And if it was by inference, so what?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מִכְּלָלָא מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the importance of the remark in Step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why it matters that שמואל's rule was inferred and not stated openly.

steps.title: In אביי's version, שמואל may have been angry for a different reason
steps.stepSummary: According to אביי's version, שמואל's anger may have been about keeping forbidden food around, not about deceiving the ferryman.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who says it was a טרפה, שמואל may have said to him: "Why did you keep forbidden food in your possession?"
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: in אביי's version, שמואל's anger has another possible explanation, so the story does not clearly prove the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the chicken was a טרפה, שמואל might have been upset that his attendant kept a forbidden item at all, not that he fooled the ferryman. So a rule worked out from a story is less certain. It depends on reading the reason correctly.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the one who says
To keep, to leave lying around

steps.whatToRemember: The rule against deceiving people, even a גוי, is attributed to שמואל. It comes from a story, so in אביי's version his anger could instead have been about keeping forbidden food.
steps.confusionAlert: This answer does not reject the rule against deceiving people. It only shows that the story could be read another way in one version, so the proof is weaker than a direct statement.

phrases.english: According to the one who says it was a טרפה,
שמואל may have said to him:
"Why did you keep forbidden food in your possession?"

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמַאן דְּאָמַר טְרֵפָה הֲוַאי, אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַמַּאי תְּשַׁהֵא אִיסּוּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 11 by showing the inference can be read another way.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: In אביי's version, שמואל's anger may have been about keeping a forbidden item, so the rule against deception is not certain from the story.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Weakens the proof from the story only in אביי's version.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The story allows a second explanation for שמואל's anger.

steps.title: In רבא's version, the anger may have been about disobeying
steps.stepSummary: According to רבא's version, שמואל asked for undiluted wine, so his anger could simply be because the attendant did not follow his instruction.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to the one who said that שמואל told him to give the ferryman a drink from an אנפקא: saying אנפקא implies undiluted wine. So שמואל may have been angry only because his order was ignored.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer. It shows that רבא's version of the story also does not have to be about deceiving the ferryman.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 12 the גמרא explained אביי's version a different way. Now it does the same for רבא's version: שמואל clearly asked for strong wine, and the attendant ignored him. That is why the rule against deceiving can only be inferred from the story, not proven.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'alive.' Here it means undiluted, full-strength wine

steps.whatToRemember: Neither version of the ferryman story proves for certain that שמואל was angry about deceiving. That is why the rule is only learned by inference.

phrases.english: According to the one who said "anpaka"
phrases.notes: This is רבא's version from step 10.

phrases.english: he told him to give the ferryman a drink
"anpaka" implies undiluted wine.
phrases.notes: The גמרא doesn't say the ending out loud: so the attendant disobeyed, and that alone could explain the anger.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמַאן דְּאָמַר אַנְפָּקָא אֲמַר לֵיהּ לְאַשְׁקוֹיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer begun in step 12 by covering רבא's version too.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: In רבא's version, שמואל's anger may have been about disobeying his instruction, not about deceiving.

steps.title: Don't make fake invitations or fake gift offers
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר teaches that you should not push someone to eat with you, or offer many gifts, when you know he will refuse.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is taught: רבי מאיר would say: A person should not press his friend to eat with him when he knows his friend won't eat. And he should not offer him many gifts when he knows his friend won't accept them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא of רבי מאיר about other kinds of misleading people. This first part covers fake invitations and fake gift offers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is creating false gratitude. The other person thinks you really wanted to host him or give to him, but you only offered because you knew he would say no. This is a form of גניבת דעת.
steps.confusionAlert: Inviting people is not the problem. The problem is an invitation you only make because you know it will be turned down.

phrases.english: It is taught: Rabbi Meir would say:
A person should not press his friend
to eat with him
when he knows that his friend will not eat
and he should not offer him many gifts
when he knows that his friend will not accept them

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, הָיָה רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the שמואל story to a related ברייתא about misleading people.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not make invitations or gift offers you know will be refused, because that creates false gratitude.

steps.title: Sold barrels, an empty oil jug, and the honor exception
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר continues: don't open already-sold barrels for a guest without telling him, and don't offer oil from an empty jug. But if it is done for the guest's honor, it is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he should not open barrels for him that are already sold to a storekeeper, unless he tells him. And he should not say to him 'anoint yourself with oil' from an empty jug. But if it is for his honor, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with two more cases of misleading a guest. Then it adds an exception for honoring the guest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Opening a barrel for a guest looks like a big loss for his sake. If the barrel was going to be opened anyway for the storekeeper, the guest gets a false impression unless he is told. Offering oil from an empty jug is the same kind of empty gesture. If the goal is to honor the guest and not to trick him, it is allowed.

phrases.english: And he should not open barrels for him
that are already sold to a storekeeper
unless he tells him
And he should not say to him, "Anoint yourself with oil"
from an empty jug
But if it is for his honor, it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא יִפְתַּח לוֹ חָבִיּוֹת הַמְּכוּרוֹת לְחֶנְוָנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא of רבי מאיר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Don't open sold barrels for a guest without telling him, and don't offer oil from an empty jug. Doing it for the guest's honor is allowed.
steps.whyThisMatters: The sold-barrels case is the one the גמרא will challenge next.

steps.title: But רב יהודה opened sold barrels for עולא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rule: רב יהודה opened barrels for עולא that were already sold to a storekeeper.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But עולא came to רב יהודה's house, and רב יהודה opened for him barrels that were sold to a storekeeper!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the barrel rule with a story about a great sage who seems to have done exactly what the ברייתא forbids.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If opening sold barrels for a guest is misleading, how could רב יהודה do it for עולא? The story seems to go against רבי מאיר's ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so? The גמרא uses this to start a challenge
Happened to come, arrived as a guest

phrases.english: Is that so?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא עוּלָּא אִיקְּלַע לְבֵי רַב יְהוּדָה
phrases.english: But Ulla came to the house of Rav Yehuda
and he opened for him barrels sold to a storekeeper!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי? וְהָא עוּלָּא אִיקְּלַע לְבֵי רַב יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the sold-barrels rule from step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule not to open sold barrels for a guest without telling him
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A great sage did exactly this, so it seems to be allowed.

steps.title: רב יהודה told him
steps.stepSummary: Answer: רב יהודה did tell עולא that the barrels were already sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: He did tell him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the story fits the ברייתא, because רב יהודה told עולא about the barrels.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא itself allows it if the host tells the guest. So רב יהודה was using the exception the ברייתא already gives.

phrases.english: He did tell him.
phrases.notes: This matches the ברייתא's words "unless he tells him" from step 15.

steps.triggerLanguage: אוֹדוֹעֵי אוֹדְעֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the story as fitting the 'unless he tells him' clause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב יהודה secretly opened sold barrels and broke the rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: He told עולא, so there was no false impression.

steps.title: עולא was so dear that רב יהודה would have opened barrels anyway
steps.stepSummary: Second answer: עולא was so beloved to רב יהודה that he would have opened barrels for him even if they weren't sold, so there was no misleading.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: עולא is different, because he was dear to רב יהודה. Even without this, he would have opened barrels for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer. Because רב יהודה loved עולא so much, opening the barrels did not give a false impression.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is a guest thinking the host made a special sacrifice that he didn't really make. Here רב יהודה really would have opened barrels just for עולא, so the gratitude עולא felt was real and earned.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say. This brings a second answer

steps.whatToRemember: גניבת דעת means creating a false feeling of gratitude. If the host tells the guest, or would really have done it anyway, there is no problem.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:

phrases.aramaic: שָׁאנֵי עוּלָּא דְּחַבִּיב לֵיהּ לְרַב יְהוּדָה
phrases.english: Ulla is different, because he was dear to Rav Yehuda
so that even without this
phrases.notes: He means: even if the barrels had not been sold to the storekeeper.

phrases.english: he would have opened barrels for him.
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the words in square brackets are the corrected wording. The meaning stays the same.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: שָׁאנֵי עוּלָּא דְּחַבִּיב לֵיהּ לְרַב יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, different answer to the challenge in step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Making a distinction based on the special relationship
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Opening sold barrels for any guest always misleads him.
steps.terutzMaskana: With a very beloved guest there is no false impression, since the host would have opened barrels for him anyway.

steps.title: Don't bring a mourner a misleading jug of wine
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that you should not bring a mourner a mostly empty jug of wine, or top it up with water, because that misleads him. If there is a crowd present, it is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: A person should not go to a mourner's house holding a jug that is mostly empty, with a little wine sloshing inside. He also should not fill it up with water, because that misleads the mourner. But if there is a crowd there, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא with another example of misleading someone, this time a visitor to a mourner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The mourner will think he is getting a full jug of good wine, so the visitor gets credit he does not deserve. Filling it with water makes the trick even worse. When a crowd is present, the gesture honors the mourner in front of people, just like the 'for his honor' exception in step 15.

keyTerms.meaning: A jug, here a jug of wine
Rattling or sloshing, because the jug is mostly empty
He misleads him, giving a false impression
Here it means a crowd of people gathered there

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
A person may not go to a house of mourning
with a rattling jug in his hand.
And he may not fill it with water,
because he misleads him.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם יֵשׁ שָׁם חֶבֶר עִיר – מוּתָּר.
phrases.english: But if there is a crowd there, it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: לֹא יֵלֵךְ אָדָם לְבֵית הָאֵבֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another example of the misleading theme from רבי מאיר's teaching, including a similar 'for his honor' exception.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not give a mourner a false impression of a full jug of wine, unless a crowd is present and it is done for his honor.

steps.title: Don't sell a sandal from a dead animal as if it were from a slaughtered one
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא forbids selling leather from an animal that died on its own as if it came from a healthy slaughtered animal, for two reasons: it misleads, and it is dangerous.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: A person may not sell someone a sandal made from an animal that died on its own, passing it off as one made from a healthy slaughtered animal. There are two reasons: first, because he misleads him; second, because of the danger.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא about misleading someone, this time in a sale.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first reason is the same misleading problem we have been learning about: the buyer thinks he is getting better leather. The second reason is new. The animal might have died from something harmful, so the leather itself could be dangerous to wear.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal that died on its own, without שחיטה
A healthy animal that was properly slaughtered
Here it means 'as if it were', passing one thing off as another

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
A person may not sell to his fellow
a sandal from an animal that died
as if it were from a healthy slaughtered animal,
because of two things:
one, because he misleads him,
and one, because of the danger.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: לֹא יִמְכּוֹר אָדָם לַחֲבֵירוֹ סַנְדָּל שֶׁל מֵתָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another misleading case, this time in business, with an extra safety reason added.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling a sandal made from a dead animal as if it came from a slaughtered one is forbidden, both because it misleads and because it is dangerous.

steps.title: Don't send a wine barrel that looks like oil
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: do not send someone a barrel of wine with oil floating on top, which makes it look like a barrel of oil.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a person may not send his friend a barrel of wine with oil floating at its top.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives another misleading case, a gift that looks like something it is not. This rule sets up the story in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Oil floats on wine, so a thin layer on top makes the whole barrel look like oil. The person receiving it is fooled about what he got.

keyTerms.meaning: Floating at its mouth, on top

phrases.english: And a person may not send to his fellow
a barrel of wine
with oil floating at its top.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא יְשַׁגֵּר אָדָם לַחֲבֵירוֹ חָבִית שֶׁל יַיִן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with another misleading case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not send a wine barrel disguised with a layer of oil on top.

steps.title: The tragic story of the oil-topped barrel
steps.stepSummary: A story shows how harmful this trick can be. A man received such a barrel, invited guests to enjoy the oil, found it was only wine, and hanged himself in shame.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a story with someone who sent his friend a barrel of wine with oil floating on top. The friend went and invited guests to share it. They came, he found it was wine, and he hanged himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא tells a real incident to show why the rule in the last step matters so much.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man planned his hospitality around oil he thought he had. When the guests arrived and there was no oil, his embarrassment was so great that he took his own life. The story shows that misleading people is not a small thing; it can cause terrible shame.
steps.whatToRemember: Misleading someone, even with a gift, is forbidden. This story shows how much harm and shame it can cause.

phrases.english: There was an incident with one who sent to his fellow

phrases.aramaic: חָבִית שֶׁל יַיִן וְשֶׁמֶן צָף עַל פִּיהָ,
phrases.english: a barrel of wine with oil floating at its top,
and he went and invited guests to share it,
phrases.notes: The 'he' here is the friend who received the barrel, thinking it was full of oil.

phrases.english: and they came in,
he found that it was a barrel of wine,
and he hanged himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַעֲשֶׂה בְּאֶחָד שֶׁשִּׁיגֵּר לַחֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates and supports the rule in step 21 with a real incident.
steps.raayaObject: The rule against sending a wine barrel topped with oil.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A story in the ברייתא where the trick caused a man to take his own life out of shame.

steps.title: Guests may not give the host's food to his children without permission
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that guests may not hand food served to them to the host's son or daughter unless the host gives permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: And guests are not allowed to give from the food in front of them to the son or daughter of the host, unless they got permission from the host.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds a rule about how guests should behave at someone else's table.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The food was served for the guests to eat, not for them to hand out. Even giving it to the host's own children is not allowed unless the host agrees. The ברייתא does not give the reason here.

keyTerms.meaning: The host, the owner of the house

phrases.english: And the guests are not permitted to give
from what is in front of them
to the son or the daughter of the host,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נָטְלוּ רְשׁוּת מִבַּעַל הַבַּיִת.
phrases.english: unless they received permission from the host.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין הָאוֹרְחִין רַשָּׁאִין לִיתֵּן מִמַּה שֶּׁלִּפְנֵיהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The same ברייתא moves from misleading gifts to a new rule about guest manners.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Guests may not give the host's food to his children without the host's permission.

steps.title: The tragic story of the three guests
steps.stepSummary: A story shows the danger of guests handing the host's food to his child. Three people died because of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man who invited three guests during years of famine. He only had about three eggs' worth of food to serve them. The host's son came in. Each guest gave his portion to the boy. The father came and found the boy with one portion in his mouth and two in his hand. In his anger he struck the boy to the ground, and the boy died. When the mother saw this, she went up to the roof, fell, and died. The father also went up to the roof, fell, and died.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא tells a story to back up the rule from step 23, that guests may not give the host's food to his children without permission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The guests meant to be kind, but the father thought his son had grabbed the little food meant for the guests. The guests' kindness misled the father, and the result was terrible. So the rule is not just about manners. It protects people from serious harm.

keyTerms.meaning: Years of famine, when food is very scarce

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how the rules in this ברייתא are meant to protect people. A small act that misleads someone can end in disaster.

phrases.english: And there was an incident with a man who invited three guests
during years of famine,
and he did not have anything to place before them
except about three eggs' worth.
The host's son came in,

phrases.aramaic: נָטַל אֶחָד מֵהֶן חֶלְקוֹ וּנְתָנוֹ לוֹ,
phrases.english: one of the guests took his portion and gave it to him,
and the second guest did the same, and the third did the same.
The child's father came,

phrases.aramaic: מְצָאוֹ שֶׁעוֹזֵק אֶחָד בְּפִיו וּשְׁתַּיִם בְּיָדוֹ,
phrases.english: and found him holding one portion in his mouth and two in his hand,
he struck him to the ground, and the boy died.
When his mother saw this,
she went up to the roof, fell, and died,

phrases.aramaic: אַף הוּא עָלָה לַגָּג וְנָפַל וָמֵת.
phrases.english: and he too went up to the roof, fell, and died.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַעֲשֶׂה בְּאֶחָד שֶׁזִּמֵּן שְׁלֹשָׁה אוֹרְחִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real-life story to support the rule in step 23.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that guests may not give the host's food to his children without permission
steps.raayaSupportSource: A story in which doing exactly that led to three deaths

steps.title: Three lives were lost over this
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says that three Jewish lives were lost because of this matter.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב said: Because of this thing, three Jewish souls were killed.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב sums up the story by pointing out that three people died because of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On the surface he only repeats what the story already said. That makes his statement look unneeded. The גמרא will ask about this right away.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov said:
Because of this matter
phrases.notes: The guests giving the host's food to his son.

phrases.english: three Jewish souls were killed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב: עַל דָּבָר זֶה נֶהֶרְגוּ שָׁלֹשׁ נְפָשׁוֹת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A comment on the story in step 24.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three lives were lost because guests gave the host's food to his child.

steps.title: What is this statement teaching us?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's statement adds, since the story already shows that three people died.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is he teaching us?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי אליעזר בן יעקב needed to say this, since we already know from the story that three people died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes a sage does not say something just to repeat facts. So there must be a hidden lesson in his words.

keyTerms.meaning: What is he teaching us? Used when a statement seems obvious

phrases.english: What is he teaching us?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the purpose of the statement in step 25.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What new information רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's obvious-seeming statement gives us

steps.title: The whole ברייתא is רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that his statement teaches us that the whole ברייתא follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches that the whole ברייתא is the teaching of רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that his comment tells us who taught this ברייתא. It was רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His closing words are not new information about the story. They act like a signature, showing that the whole list of rules came from him. That tells us whose opinion these rules are.

keyTerms.meaning: That all of it, the whole teaching

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא about the sandal, the oil-topped wine barrel and guests' manners was all taught by רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.

phrases.aramaic: דְּכוּלַּהּ רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב הִיא.
phrases.english: That the whole of it is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's.
phrases.notes: 'The whole of it' means the whole list of rules in this ברייתא, not just the story.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּכוּלַּהּ רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 26.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The statement shows that the entire ברייתא was taught by רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.

steps.title: Sending a thigh: when must the גיד הנשה be removed?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that a whole thigh may be sent with the גיד הנשה still in it, but a cut thigh must have it removed first. A thigh sent to a גוי never needs it removed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: If someone sends a thigh to his friend and it is whole, he does not need to remove the גיד הנשה from it. If it is cut up, he must remove the גיד הנשה from it. If he sends it to a גוי, whether it is cut or whole, he does not need to remove the גיד הנשה.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא teaches when you must take out the גיד הנשה before sending a thigh to someone else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a whole thigh, the person who gets it can see the גיד הנשה is still there, so he will remove it himself. With a cut-up thigh, he may not realize it is still inside and could eat it by mistake. A גוי is not forbidden to eat the גיד הנשה, so there is nothing to worry about.

keyTerms.meaning: The sciatic nerve in the thigh, which a Jew may not eat
Thigh, the leg piece of an animal

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not whether the meat may be eaten. The question is whether the sender must remove the גיד הנשה himself so the person who gets it does not eat it by mistake.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who sends a thigh to his friend,

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלֵימָה – אֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּטּוֹל הֵימֶנָּה גִּיד הַנָּשֶׁה.
phrases.english: if it is whole, he does not need to remove the sciatic nerve from it.
If it is cut,
he needs to remove the sciatic nerve from it.
And with a gentile, whether it is cut or whole,

phrases.aramaic: אֵין צָרִיךְ לִיטּוֹל הֵימֶנָּה גִּיד הַנָּשֶׁה.
phrases.english: he does not need to remove the sciatic nerve from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַשּׁוֹלֵחַ יָרֵךְ לַחֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא, which goes back to the topic of גיד הנשה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A whole thigh may be sent with the גיד הנשה still in it. A cut thigh sent to a Jew must have it removed first. A thigh sent to a גוי never needs it removed.

steps.title: Two reasons not to sell נבילות וטריפות to a גוי
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא gives two reasons why one may not sell נבילות וטריפות to a גוי: it misleads him, and he might resell the meat to a Jew.
steps.simpleTranslation: For two reasons the רבנן said one may not sell נבילות וטריפות to a גוי. First, because it misleads him. Second, because he might sell it to another Jew.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with a rule about selling non-kosher meat to a גוי, and gives two reasons for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גוי may eat this meat, so eating it is not the problem. First, he will think he is buying good kosher meat, so he is being misled. Second, he may sell it to a Jew, who would trust it because a Jew sold it first.

keyTerms.meaning: Animals that died without a proper שחיטה
Animals with a fatal defect, which are not kosher even after שחיטה

steps.whatToRemember: Misleading people is forbidden even with a גוי, and we also worry that non-kosher meat could end up being sold to a Jew.
steps.whyThisMatters: It connects back to the theme of this whole section: you may not mislead anyone, Jew or גוי.

phrases.english: And because of two things they said
one may not sell carcasses and tereifot to a gentile:
one, because he misleads him,
and the other, lest he then go back
and sell it to another Jew.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִפְּנֵי שְׁנֵי דְבָרִים אָמְרוּ אֵין מוֹכְרִין נְבֵילוֹת וּטְרֵפוֹת לְגוֹי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with a related rule about dealing with a גוי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may not sell נבילות וטריפות to a גוי, because it misleads him and because he may resell it to a Jew.

steps.title: Do not ask a gentile to buy meat for you
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that a person should not give a גוי a דינר and ask him to buy meat with it, and says there are two reasons for this.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a person should not say to a גוי, "Take this דינר and buy me meat with it," because of two reasons.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a new rule: don't send a גוי with money to buy you meat. It is setting up the next move, because the two reasons have not been given yet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the rule right before it (not selling נבילות וטריפות to a גוי), this rule also has two reasons. Here the ברייתא only says that two reasons exist. It does not spell them out yet, so the learner should hold on and wait for the next lines.

keyTerms.meaning: A common coin of the time
Because of two reasons. A signal that two separate reasons are about to be listed.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for the two reasons inside this line. The ברייתא only announces them here and lists them in the lines that come next.

phrases.english: And a person should not say to a gentile:
"Buy meat for me with this dinar,"
because of two reasons:

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא יֹאמַר אָדָם לְגוֹי ״קַח לִי בְּדִינָר זֶה בָּשָׂר״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא. It adds a second rule about dealing with a גוי and meat, built the same way as Step 29 with two reasons.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A Jew should not give a גוי a דינר and ask him to buy meat for him. There are two reasons, which are stated next.
